title: Klezmer Modes and Dances, an Explainer
content_blocks: In this post I will very briefly describe some of the modes of traditional Klezmer. Don’t worry if you don’t understand those descriptions, though, since equally interesting are the names of the modes, which—together with the dances themselves—speak volumes about the origins of Klezmer music.

The Doyna of Prelude and Fugue No.9 from Book II is written in a mode like the Dorian mode—with ↓3, ↑6, ↓7—but with ↑4 as well, giving it that pungent augmented second between ↓3 and ↑4. It is known as the Ukrainian Dorian; in synagogue music as the Mi Shebeirach (synagogue modes are called shtaygers); and is similar to the Middle Eastern Nikriz maqqam. It is used commonly for doynas, and is typically followed by pieces written in the next mode: a mode that is like the Phrygian mode—with ↓2, ↑6, ↓7—but with ↑3 as well, thus not only giving it that pungent augmented second between ↓2 and ↑3 but making it a rotation of the Ukrainian Dorian. It is sometimes known as the Phrygian Dominant; in synagogue music as the Ahavah Rabbah shtayger; and in Klezmer music as the Freygish (as a cross between Freylekh—see below—and Phrygian, the label Freygish is both accurate and witty); and is also similar to the Hijaz-Nahawand Middle-Eastern maqqam. Lastly, we have the Mixolydian mode—with ↓7—which is called Adonai Malakh shtayger in synagogue music, and the natural minor (or Aeolian mode)—with ↓3, ↓6, ↓7—which is called the Magen Avot shtayger.

(An interesting side note about shtaygers:  they are not necessarily octave repeating, meaning that the pattern of notes in the first octave do not necessarily repeat an octave higher.  This has been an inspiration to me in the creation of many of my own original modes.)

The relationships between Klezmer, synagogue music, and local musical traditions of the countries in Eastern Europe—in an almost straight line down from Belarus, through Ukraine, Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria, and ending in western Turkey—are strongly suggested by the names of the modes seen above. These same relationships exist with the dances forms, as well. The Doyna emerges from a Romanian and Middle Eastern tradition of the doina; the Freylekh is found in Belarus, and the Hora is a dance found widely from Moldova down through Romania, Bulgaria, Macedonia, Greece, and Turkey. Other Klezmer dances are given purely geographical names, such as the Bulgar (from Bulgaria and Moldova) and the Terkisher (from Turkey).

So, if the Klezmer dances, musical forms, and modes all emerged from a blending of Eastern European and Middle Eastern music with Jewish secular and liturgical music, what differentiates Klezmer from those local traditions? My answer is the krekhts discussed in the previous blog post.
Ukrainian Dorian, Bulgar, Terkisher Tanz, down to Freylekhs, Horas, and Doinas, all speak volumes about the debt Klezmer owes to its geographical neighbors.
